topic: Forces and motion: Forces, accelerations and Newton's Laws of motion
subject: physics

items.q: A crate rests on a level floor. Its weight is 400 N downwards and the floor pushes up on it with a force of 400 N. Which statement about the crate is correct?
items.correct: The resultant force on it is zero, so it stays stationary.
items.misconception: No forces act on it at all, and that is why it stays still.
items.why: Forces are introduced as pushes and pulls that make things happen, so a situation where nothing happens looks like a situation with no forces. Weight and the contact force from a surface are also invisible. Newton's First Law is about the resultant force being zero, not about there being no forces. Draw every force on the object first, then decide what their resultant is.
items.random_wrong: Its weight and the floor's push are a third law pair.

items.q: A puck slides across a level ice rink in a straight line at a steady 4 m/s. Friction and air resistance are so small they can be ignored. What is the resultant force on the puck?
items.correct: It is zero, because the puck's velocity is not changing.
items.misconception: It acts forwards, because the puck is still moving forwards.
items.why: Every moving object in ordinary life does stop, because friction and air resistance act on it. Students generalise from that experience and treat motion, rather than change of motion, as the thing needing a cause. A force changes velocity; it does not maintain it. Remove friction and air resistance and the puck keeps its velocity for ever with no forward force at all.
items.random_wrong: It acts backwards, so the puck is gradually slowing down.

items.q: A lorry travels along a straight, level motorway at a constant 25 m/s. What is true of the horizontal forces on it?
items.correct: The driving force and the resistive forces are equal.
items.misconception: The driving force is larger than the resistive forces.
items.why: The engine is obviously doing something, and students expect the direction of travel to belong to the larger force. Fuel is being used, so it feels as though the forward force must be winning. A larger driving force would give a resultant force forwards, and the lorry would be speeding up. Constant speed in a straight line means zero resultant force, so the forces are exactly equal.
items.random_wrong: The resistive forces are larger than the driving force.

items.q: A car is driven round a roundabout at a constant speed of 8 m/s. Is there a resultant force acting on the car?
items.correct: Yes, because its direction, and so its velocity, is changing.
items.misconception: No, because its speed stays the same all the way round.
items.why: Students use 'speed' and 'velocity' as synonyms in everyday talk, so a constant speedometer reading looks like unchanging motion. Velocity is speed and/or direction. Change either one and the velocity has changed, which requires a resultant force - here one directed towards the centre of the roundabout.
items.random_wrong: No, but a forward force is needed to keep the car moving.

items.q: A skydiver falls at a steady terminal velocity before opening her parachute. Which statement explains this using Newton's First Law?
items.correct: Air resistance now equals her weight, so the resultant force is zero and her velocity is constant.
items.misconception: Her weight is still larger than air resistance, and that is what keeps her moving down.
items.why: Every moving object in ordinary life does stop, because friction and air resistance act on it. Students generalise from that experience and treat motion, rather than change of motion, as the thing needing a cause. A force changes velocity; it does not maintain it. Remove friction and air resistance and the puck keeps its velocity for ever with no forward force at all.
items.random_wrong: Air resistance is now larger than her weight, so she is gradually pushed back upwards.

items.q: A train is braking as it comes into a station. Which statement about the forces on the train is correct?
items.correct: The resultant force acts backwards, opposite to the direction of travel.
items.misconception: The forward force is smaller now but still larger than the braking force.
items.why: Every moving object in ordinary life does stop, because friction and air resistance act on it. Students generalise from that experience and treat motion, rather than change of motion, as the thing needing a cause. A force changes velocity; it does not maintain it. Remove friction and air resistance and the puck keeps its velocity for ever with no forward force at all.
items.random_wrong: The forces are now balanced, and balanced forces are what bring it to rest.

items.q: The tendency of an object to continue in its state of rest or of uniform motion has a name. Which statement gives it correctly?
items.correct: Inertia, which is the tendency to stay at rest or in uniform motion.
items.misconception: Inertia, which is the force that keeps a moving object going forwards.
items.why: The word is used in everyday speech as though it were a push, and it is introduced alongside forces. Students still looking for a cause of continued motion seize on it as that cause. Inertia is a property, not a force. It never appears on a free body diagram and it is never measured in newtons. Continued motion needs no cause; only a change of motion does.
items.random_wrong: Momentum, which is a property an object has only while it is moving.

items.q: Which statement of Newton's Second Law is correct?
items.correct: Acceleration is proportional to resultant force and inversely proportional to mass.
items.misconception: Acceleration is proportional to resultant force and proportional to mass.
items.why: 'Proportional' is remembered from the first half of the sentence and applied to both quantities. In F = m a the mass and the acceleration sit side by side, which looks like a direct relationship. Read the law in two halves: acceleration is proportional to resultant force, and inversely proportional to mass. Rearranged, a = F / m - mass is on the bottom, so more mass means less acceleration.
items.random_wrong: Acceleration is proportional to mass and inversely proportional to force.

items.q: Which equation is Newton's Second Law as the specification states it?
items.correct: resultant force = mass x acceleration
items.misconception: acceleration = mass x resultant force
items.why: 'Proportional' is remembered from the first half of the sentence and applied to both quantities. In F = m a the mass and the acceleration sit side by side, which looks like a direct relationship. Read the law in two halves: acceleration is proportional to resultant force, and inversely proportional to mass. Rearranged, a = F / m - mass is on the bottom, so more mass means less acceleration.
items.random_wrong: mass = resultant force x acceleration

items.q: Which set of units is correct for the quantities in F = m a?
items.correct: F in N, m in kg, a in m/s²
items.misconception: F in N, m in kg, a in m/s
items.why: Speed and velocity are met first and both use m/s, so m/s becomes the default unit for anything to do with motion; the squared sign looks like a decoration. Acceleration tells you how many metres per second the velocity changes in each second, so its unit is (m/s) per s, written m/s². Only that unit gives newtons when multiplied by kilograms.
items.random_wrong: F in N, m in N, a in m/s²

items.q: A trolley of mass 0.80 kg has a resultant force of 2.0 N acting on it. What is its acceleration?
items.correct: 2.5 m/s²
items.misconception: 1.6 m/s²
items.why: Students remember F = m a as 'the numbers multiply' and, unsure how to rearrange, multiply whatever they are given rather than dividing. Cover the quantity you want in the formula triangle, or divide both sides by a. Check the answer by substituting back: 15 x 4.0 = 60 N, which matches, while 240 x 4.0 = 960 N does not.

items.q: A car of mass 1200 kg has a driving force of 4800 N and resistive forces of 1800 N acting on it. What is its acceleration?
items.correct: 2.5 m/s²
items.misconception: 4.0 m/s²
items.why: The driving force is the one that looks responsible for the motion, and questions often name it first. The word 'resultant' is easily skipped when reading the equation. F in the equation is always the resultant of all the forces acting. Work out the resultant first, then substitute; using 4800 N here would overstate the acceleration by 60 per cent.
items.random_wrong: 5.5 m/s²

items.q: A resultant force of 60 N gives an object an acceleration of 4.0 m/s². What is the mass of the object?
items.correct: 15 kg
items.misconception: 240 kg
items.why: Students remember F = m a as 'the numbers multiply' and, unsure how to rearrange, multiply whatever they are given rather than dividing. Cover the quantity you want in the formula triangle, or divide both sides by a. Check the answer by substituting back: 15 x 4.0 = 60 N, which matches, while 240 x 4.0 = 960 N does not.

items.q: The resultant force on an object is doubled, and at the same time its mass is doubled. What happens to its acceleration?
items.correct: It stays the same, as the two changes cancel each other out.
items.misconception: It is four times as large, as both changes increase it.
items.why: 'Proportional' is remembered from the first half of the sentence and applied to both quantities. In F = m a the mass and the acceleration sit side by side, which looks like a direct relationship. Read the law in two halves: acceleration is proportional to resultant force, and inversely proportional to mass. Rearranged, a = F / m - mass is on the bottom, so more mass means less acceleration.
items.random_wrong: It is halved, because the greater mass has the bigger effect.

items.q: Two trolleys are pushed with the same resultant force. Trolley A proves much harder to speed up than trolley B. What does this show?
items.correct: Trolley A has the greater inertial mass of the two.
items.misconception: Trolley A has a larger inertia force acting on it.
items.why: The word is used in everyday speech as though it were a push, and it is introduced alongside forces. Students still looking for a cause of continued motion seize on it as that cause. Inertia is a property, not a force. It never appears on a free body diagram and it is never measured in newtons. Continued motion needs no cause; only a change of motion does.
items.random_wrong: Trolley A weighs more, and weight is what resists.

items.q: How is inertial mass defined, and what unit does it have?
items.correct: The ratio of force over acceleration, measured in kg.
items.misconception: The force needed to hold an object still, measured in N.
items.why: The word 'force' appears in the definition, and students expect the unit of a defined quantity to be the unit of the first quantity named in it. Dividing changes the unit. Inertial mass is a mass and is measured in kilograms; if it came out in newtons it could not be substituted for m in F = m a.
items.random_wrong: The ratio of acceleration over force, measured in kg.

items.q: A family car of mass about 1200 kg accelerates hard, reaching 27 m/s from rest in about 9 s. Estimate the resultant force on the car.
items.why: The speed is the number the question gives most prominently, and students who have not separated speed from acceleration take the largest available figure for 'how fast it speeds up'. Acceleration is a rate of change of velocity, so it must be found by dividing a change of velocity by a time. Substituting the speed instead of the acceleration inflates the force roughly ninefold here.

items.q: A car pulls away from traffic lights and reaches 13 m/s in about 6 s. Which is the best estimate of its acceleration?
items.correct: ~ 2 m/s²
items.misconception: ~ 78 m/s²
items.why: Students remember F = m a as 'the numbers multiply' and, unsure how to rearrange, multiply whatever they are given rather than dividing. Cover the quantity you want in the formula triangle, or divide both sides by a. Check the answer by substituting back: 15 x 4.0 = 60 N, which matches, while 240 x 4.0 = 960 N does not.
items.random_wrong: ~ 13 m/s²

items.q: A student writes 'resultant force ~ 4000 N' at the end of a calculation. What does the symbol tell the reader?
items.correct: That the value is approximate rather than exact.
items.misconception: That the value is a guess, so precision was not needed.
items.why: 'Approximate' sounds like permission to be vague, and estimates are set without exact data, so students think no method is expected. An estimate is calculated from an equation using rounded but sensible values, and is then quoted to one or two significant figures with the symbol in front. A wildly wrong order of magnitude is still wrong.
items.random_wrong: That the value was not worked out from an equation.

items.q: In Required practical activity 7, a student investigates how the resultant force affects the acceleration of a trolley. What must be kept constant?
items.correct: The total mass accelerated, trolley and hanging masses.
items.misconception: Only the mass of the trolley, not the hanging masses.
items.why: The trolley is the object students are watching, and the hanging masses look like part of the apparatus that supplies the force rather than part of the moving system. The string makes the trolley and the hanging masses accelerate together as one system, so their combined mass is the m in F = m a. Transferring masses raises the force while holding that total fixed.
items.random_wrong: The friction, which is small enough to ignore here.

items.q: In the second part of Required practical activity 7 the accelerating force is kept constant while masses are added to the trolley. What happens, and what shape is a graph of acceleration against mass?
items.correct: Acceleration falls, and the graph is a curve, not a straight line.
items.misconception: Acceleration falls, and the graph is a straight line sloping down.
items.why: Students treat any relationship where one quantity falls as the other rises as linear, and a straight line is the easiest line of best fit to draw. Doubling the mass halves the acceleration rather than reducing it by a fixed amount, which gives a curve. Plot acceleration against 1 / mass and the points fall on a straight line through the origin.
items.random_wrong: Acceleration rises, and the graph is a straight line sloping up.

items.q: A student plots acceleration against resultant force for a trolley of constant mass. The line of best fit is straight but crosses the force axis at 0.4 N instead of passing through the origin. What is the most likely reason?
items.correct: Friction on the runway was not properly compensated for.
items.misconception: Friction can be ignored, so the intercept must be a plotting slip.
items.why: The trolley runs freely and the friction is not visible, and textbook questions routinely say 'ignore friction'. The tilt then looks like an odd extra step. Uncompensated friction means part of the pull is used up opposing it, so the measured acceleration is too small and the graph of acceleration against force cuts the force axis instead of passing through the origin.
items.random_wrong: The hanging masses were not counted in the mass accelerated.

items.q: Two objects interact. What does Newton's Third Law say about the forces they exert on each other?
items.correct: They are equal in size and opposite in direction.
items.misconception: The first object acts and the second one reacts just after.
items.why: The old wording 'action and reaction' suggests a sequence, and in everyday language a reaction is a response to something that has already happened. Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite - simultaneously. There is no delay and no way to say which force caused the other.
items.random_wrong: The larger object exerts the larger of the two forces.

items.q: A person stands still on a floor. Which two forces form a Newton's Third Law pair?
items.correct: The floor pushes up on the person; the person pushes down on the floor.
items.misconception: The floor pushes up on the person; gravity pulls the person down.
items.why: The two forces are the ones drawn on the diagram, and they really are equal and opposite here, so the definition seems to fit. A Third Law pair acts on two different objects and is always the same type of force. The partner of the table's push on the book is the book's push on the table; the partner of the book's weight is the book's gravitational pull on the Earth.
items.random_wrong: The person pushes down on the floor; friction acts sideways on them.

items.q: A car collides head-on with a much heavier lorry. Which statement about the forces during the collision is correct?
items.correct: The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
items.misconception: The lorry exerts the larger force because it has far more mass.
items.why: The damage is far worse on the car, and students read the outcome back into the forces. Everyday language about a heavy vehicle 'hitting harder' reinforces it. The forces are equal; the accelerations are not. The same size force produces a much larger acceleration on the smaller mass, which is why the car is damaged more.
items.random_wrong: The forces cancel out, so neither vehicle changes its velocity.

items.q: Why can the two forces in a Newton's Third Law pair never cancel each other out?
items.correct: They act on two different objects, and not on the same one.
items.misconception: They act at different times, so they are never present together.
items.why: The old wording 'action and reaction' suggests a sequence, and in everyday language a reaction is a response to something that has already happened. Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite - simultaneously. There is no delay and no way to say which force caused the other.
items.random_wrong: They are not truly equal in size, only roughly the same size.

items.q: The forces on a moving trolley are balanced. What happens to it?
items.correct: It continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction, so at the same velocity.
items.misconception: Balanced forces bring a moving object to a stop.
items.why: Students meet balanced forces first in examples of stationary objects, so 'balanced' becomes attached to 'at rest'. Real trolleys also do stop, because the forces on them are not in fact balanced. Zero resultant force means no change of velocity. If the trolley was moving at 2 m/s it goes on at 2 m/s; only a resultant force could slow it down.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: The same resultant force acts on a heavy trolley and a light trolley. Which accelerates more?
items.correct: The light one. Acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass of the object.
items.misconception: The heavy one, because heavy things have more force behind them.
items.why: Students confuse the resultant force with the object's weight, and know that heavy objects fall hard and hit hard, so they associate mass with a bigger effect rather than with resistance to change. The resultant force is stated to be the same for both. In a = F / m, increasing m with F fixed makes a smaller, so the heavier trolley accelerates less.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: An object weighs 12 N on Earth. What value of m goes into F = m a?
items.correct: Not 12. The mass must be in kilograms; a weight in newtons is a force, not a mass.
items.misconception: The mass is 12, since that is the number given for how heavy it is.
items.why: In everyday English 'weight' and 'mass' mean the same thing, and both are quoted as single numbers describing how heavy something is. Mass is measured in kilograms and does not change; weight is a force in newtons. Only a mass in kg may be substituted for m, and grams must be converted first.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the inertial mass of a trolley the same as the mass you would measure on a balance?
items.correct: Yes. Inertial mass is that same mass, described by how hard it is to change the object's velocity.
items.misconception: Inertial mass is a separate quantity that an object only has when it is being accelerated.
items.why: The word 'inertial' makes it sound like a new quantity, and it is introduced through an experiment about acceleration, so it seems to belong only to moving objects. Inertial mass is a way of defining mass, not a second kind of mass. A 2 kg trolley has an inertial mass of 2 kg whether it is at rest or accelerating.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If the forces in a Newton's Third Law pair are equal and opposite, why does anything ever accelerate?
items.correct: Because the two forces act on two different objects, so they never appear in the same resultant.
items.misconception: They must cancel out, so no object could ever have a resultant force on it.
items.why: Students learn to cancel equal and opposite forces when finding a resultant, and apply that habit without checking which object each force acts on. Only forces acting on the same object can be combined into a resultant. A horse pulls the cart and the cart pulls the horse; the cart's motion depends only on the forces acting on the cart.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Roughly what resultant force accelerates a family car briskly away from traffic lights?
items.correct: Of the order of a few thousand newtons - around 4000 N for a 1200 kg car at about 3 m/s².
items.misconception: A few hundred newtons, because that already sounds like a big push.
items.why: The only forces students have handled are weights of laboratory masses, a few newtons at most, so a few hundred newtons feels enormous by comparison. Multiply through: a car's mass is around a thousand kilograms, so even a modest acceleration of 3 m/s² needs thousands of newtons. Always finish the estimate with F = m a rather than judging by feel.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A car has a driving force of 4800 N forwards and resistive forces of 1800 N backwards. What is the resultant force?
items.correct: 3000 N forwards - the forces are in opposite directions, so they subtract.
items.misconception: 6600 N, because you add the two forces together to get the total.
items.why: 'Resultant' is heard as 'total', and adding is the operation students default to when two numbers are given for the same quantity. Direction decides the operation. Forces in the same direction add; forces in opposite directions subtract, and the resultant acts in the direction of the larger force.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is any pair of equal and opposite forces a Newton's Third Law pair?
items.correct: No. The two forces must act on two different objects, and be the same type of force.
items.misconception: If two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, that is what makes them a Third Law pair.
items.why: The law is usually remembered as the phrase 'equal and opposite', and the rest of the definition - two objects, one interaction - is dropped. Ask which object each force acts on. Two forces on the same object are balanced forces under the First Law; a Third Law pair always comes from one interaction between two objects.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.5.6.2 Forces and motion: Forces, accelerations and Newton's Laws of motion
